HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn
intro: HTTP Request Smuggling is an advanced technique for attacking websites that have one or more front-end servers. An attack is launched by sending ambiguous HTTP requests that get interpreted as different lengths by the servers. This causes them to desynchronize, and merge requests and responses from attackers and legitimate users. This can ultimately lead to a wide range of serious effects. These include letting attackers steal plaintext passwords, and poison caches to persistently compromise critical functionality like login pages. It was first documented in 2004, but largely forgotten until we revisited it in 2019. We built on the existing request smuggling research with modern techniques and tooling, earning six figures in bug bounties along the way. We presented HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn at both Black Hat USA and DEF CON. This repopularized the technique, and has since led to a wave of discoveries and patches. In subsequent years we presented HTTP/2: The Sequel is Always Worse followed by Browser-Powered Desync Attacks. The next major installment will be HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame. We also released a collection of interactive labs as part of our Web Security Academy, so you can practise applying the techniques to real systems.

title: Template Injection Research
headings: Adapting AngularJS payloads to exploit real world applications
XSS without HTML: Client-Side Template Injection with AngularJS
intro: Template injection occurs when user input is able to define template expressions. It's commonly classified into two types. These are known as Client side template injection and Server side template injection. Client side template injection usually occurs within the browser and HTML. It happens because a developer allows user input within a webpage, and allows them to define template expressions. This then allows an attacker to inject template expressions (which are simplified JavaScript) to exploit the web application. This is similar to how Cross Site Scripting works. Some JavaScript frameworks, such as AngularJS, have a sandbox - this prevents a developer from using certain objects that they weren't supposed to. In order for an attacker to exploit this, they need to find a way to "escape" the sandbox. This means gaining access to areas such as the document object, in order to exploit the web application. If you're looking for the latest techniques and vectors related to CSTI then we've got you covered. You can learn how we broke the AngularJS sandbox step by step, and even try it out for yourself with our interactive labs. We'll show you how we exploited real world applications, even with severe restrictions in place. title: Probably Not Exploitable
headings: Not panic. More like a low hum.

What would you do with the time?
intro: If you've worked in security for any length of time, you've definitely turned to a colleague and said some version of "this probably isn't exploitable" and moved on. Usually late in the day, with a few dozen other findings waiting and a release going out in the morning. But nobody says it because they don't care. They say it because there are only so many man hours in the week, and the queue keeps refilling. We wanted to know how common that assumption really is, and how people feel about the pile of work it creates. So we decided to find out for ourselves. We went out and surveyed 214 security practitioners and leaders to learn more, and they were more candid than we expected. 44% told us they close or deprioritize findings without fully verifying them because they don't have time. Only 36% said that doesn't happen on their team. And the group most likely to admit it was CISOs and security leaders, at 54%. That last number was surprising. This isn't something happening quietly behind leadership's back. It's the normal state of things, and the people running these programs & teams know it better than anyone. When we asked people how they feel about their backlog, the most common answer by far was "manageable, but always in the back of my mind." Nearly half (47%) picked it.

title: The Exposure Debt Benchmark: What the 2026 Data Says About the Find-to-Fix Gap

intro: Somewhere in a security team's vulnerability backlog right now, a confirmed vulnerability is waiting to be fixed. Whether uncovered by a security researcher or through agentic security testing, the finding has been validated and its potential impact assessed. Yet despite security teams resolving vulnerabilities faster than ever, this one remains open, with more findings arriving every week. According to HackerOne's Security Research Report 2026, Exposure Debt: The Next Challenge in Cybersecurity, valid vulnerability reports awaiting resolution grew 131% between 2024 and 2026, even as the reports that did get fixed moved through the system more than twice as fast. So why, when the average resolution time fell from 135 days to 62 for all severities, is there such a gap between what gets found and what gets fixed? The short answer is that discovery has outrun remediation, and what it leaves behind is exposure debt, the growing gap between the vulnerabilities an organization finds and the ones it can fix. Like any debt, it compounds, with each unresolved finding extending the window in which an attacker can act. A backlog that grows 131% while resolution time falls by more than half sounds like a contradiction, but the explanation comes down to arithmetic. Part of the drop likely reflects real progress, such as tighter workflows, clearer ownership, and faster routing to engineers.

intro: The National Vulnerability Database (NVD), run by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), is a foundational resource that security teams across the public and private sectors use to track software flaws. As artificial intelligence (AI) changes how vulnerabilities are found and exploited, NIST asked for input on modernizing the NVD. HackerOne filed comments on October 13, 2026. Our central message: AI can scale proven processes and focus human expertise. Finding more vulnerabilities only improves security if organizations can validate and fix them, but that is where systems are now breaking down. On the H1 Platform, the backlog of validated, unresolved vulnerabilities grew 131% in two years, even as average resolution time improved 54% over the same period. The answer is not to replace security professionals, but to equip their processes to handle higher volume. AI is well suited to repeatable work such as initial triage, spotting duplicates, and connecting information across reports. That frees people to focus on findings that are novel, ambiguous, or dependent on a specific environment, where their judgment is irreplaceable. Human reviewers should be able to see the underlying evidence and challenge an AI-generated conclusion. NIST should not create separate processes for AI-discovered vulnerabilities. Asked about delegating security decisions to AI, 47% named accuracy as their top concern, specifically false negatives: real vulnerabilities an AI tool rejects or misjudges, which then go unaddressed. intro: We evaluate each new frontier model against the hardest thing our remediation product does: write a security fix an engineer will trust and merge. This post is about how we built an evaluation we can trust, and how a trustworthy measurement changed what we could improve. Critical vulnerabilities are being resolved faster than ever. On the H1 Platform, average resolution time for critical reports fell 61% between June 2024 and June 2026. Over the same period, open valid reports across all severities grew 131%, and open critical reports grew 123%. Speed gains are real, but volume is outpacing them. The value now concentrates on what happens next: turning a validated finding into a verified fix that an engineer reviews, accepts, and merges. That is why organizations are focusing more on remediation as part of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): find the vulnerability, validate it, find the root cause, remediate it, confirm the fix held, repeat. Remediation is the step where risk actually comes down, so it is the step we hold to the highest bar. We evaluate frontier models against that bar. For this first update, we’re looking back at changes made through July. We plan to publish these quarterly, with the next update expected in November (Q3). Before you spend time on a program, you should be able to understand what is in scope, what is excluded, and what rewards apply. We added a Hacker API endpoint that lets researchers retrieve the report categories a program excludes from rewards. That means you can bring those exclusions into your own research and automation workflows before you test or submit.

title: ZIP Parser Differentials and Mutable Encrypted Filenames - Part I
headings: How a ZIP File is Structured
Scenario A: Gateway reads central directory, user extracts with libarchive
Scenario B: Gateway uses libarchive, user extracts with unzip/7-Zip/Explorer
intro: When you password-protect a ZIP file, you probably assume the entire thing is locked. The contents are encrypted, sure, but the filenames are not. They sit in plaintext, in two separate records, and nothing stops you from editing them without the password. That is interesting on its own. It gets more interesting when you realize that different ZIP implementations disagree on which of those two filename records to trust. Info-ZIP and 7-Zip read the central directory. Libarchive reads the local header. If a security tool and a user’s extraction utility are on opposite sides of that split, they are literally looking at different filenames for the same encrypted entry. This is Part 1 of a two-part series. Here I document the primitive: how ZIP filename metadata can be modified in encrypted archives, why the two filename records exist, and what happens when different tools parse a deliberately inconsistent archive. The goal is to establish and validate the underlying condition, i.e. the parser disagreement, so that Part 2 can test it against a real security boundary. Two structures carry the filename: the local file header, which sits right before the entry’s data, and the central directory, which is an index at the end of the archive.
